title: Further Rates of Change

findings.finding: The opening lacks rehearsal of polynomial differentiation, which the worked example uses directly before introducing the connection between rates.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall and evaluate a polynomial derivative while learning to choose the related-rate chain.
findings.checked: Teaching is complete. No opening review precedes p3-example-item, and no earlier topic supplies rehearsal. Polynomial differentiation is a substantial prerequisite used directly in the worked solution.
findings.assumptions: Polynomial differentiation is prior Stage 6 knowledge. Calculator availability does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Before p3-theory, add: (a) Differentiate y=3x²−4x+2. Answer: 6x−4. (b) Differentiate y=x³+x. Answer: 3x²+1. (c) For y=2x²−x, find dy/dx at x=3. Answer: 11. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse differentiation and derivative evaluation before the related-rate example.

findings.finding: Extend p4-q4 to compare how the input rate changes the output rate at a fixed value of x.
findings.breakdown: At x=3, dA/dx=4, so the output rate is four times the input rate, including negative and zero rates.
findings.checked: For A=16x−2x², dA/dx=16−4x=4 at x=3. All proposed answers follow by multiplying dx/dt by 4. The supplied practice has no comparable run.
findings.assumptions: Use the existing formula and x=3 throughout; no additional method is needed.

repair.proposal: Label the existing task (a), then add one instruction: “Predict each rate before calculating.” Add further parts asking for dA/dt when dx/dt is (b) 1, (c) 2, (d) −2, (e) 0. Answers: 4, 8, −8, 0. Follow with (f) dx/dt=3.5. Answer: 14. Only dx/dt varies; A(x) and x remain fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts expose the fixed multiplier linking the two rates.

findings.finding: The opening review recalls geometric formulas but does not rehearse isolating a squared or cubed length through a π coefficient, as required by the inverse-rate example.
findings.breakdown: In p9-example-body, obtaining r from 36π=(4/3)πr³ is a prerequisite step before evaluating the radius rate.
findings.checked: The complete preceding teaching and supplied preceding practice do not rehearse solving these equations. The missing piece is cancelling the coefficient and isolating the power, rather than calculator evaluation of a root.
findings.assumptions: Solving elementary geometric equations is prior knowledge. Positive lengths are intended.

repair.proposal: Append to p5-review-block: “Find the positive length in each equation.” (g) πr²=25π. Answer: r=5. (h) 4πr²=144π. Answer: r=6. (i) (4/3)πr³=288π. Answer: r=6. Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses isolating squared and cubed lengths before the inverse-rate example.

findings.finding: Extend the balloon question to compare volumes when the inflow doubles while the surface-area rate remains fixed.
findings.breakdown: With dA/dt=1, the related rates give dV/dt=r/2. Doubling inflow therefore doubles radius and multiplies volume by eight.
findings.checked: Using A=4πr² and V=(4/3)πr³ gives dr/dt=1/(8πr) and dV/dt=r/2. An inflow of 20 cm³/s gives r=40 cm and V=256000π/3 cm³, eight times the volume in part (b). These methods are available within the topic.
findings.assumptions: The balloon remains spherical and the original constant surface-area rate continues.

repair.proposal: After p15-q17-b, add (c) “Find the volume when water is flowing in at 20 cm³/s.” Answer: 256000π/3 cm³. Add (d) “How many times the volume in part (b) is this?” Answer: 8 times.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects the fixed surface-area rate with the scaling of radius and volume.

findings.finding: The review rehearses forming similar-triangle ratios but omits solving a linear equation with the dependent variable on both sides, which the shadow example uses directly.
findings.breakdown: Students must turn s/(s+x)=2/20 into s=x/9 before differentiation; forming the ratio alone does not rehearse that algebraic step.
findings.checked: p17-review-q2 includes rearranging trigonometric expressions, but neither it nor the preceding topic rehearses collecting an unknown from both sides. The shadow solution explicitly requires expansion and collection in 20s=2s+2x.
findings.assumptions: Linear equation solving is prior Stage 6 knowledge. Calculator availability is immaterial.

repair.proposal: Append three short items to p17-review-q3-block: (a) Make s the subject of 8s=2(s+x). Answer: s=x/3. (b) Make s the subject of s/(s+x)=3/15. Answer: s=x/4. (c) Make s the subject of s/(s+x)=4/10. Answer: s=2x/3. Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses clearing a denominator and collecting the dependent variable before the shadow example.

findings.finding: Extend the trough question to compare the inflows required for the same depth increase at two depths.
findings.breakdown: For a fixed depth rate, dV/dt=2000h(dh/dt) increases with depth, while dA/dt=2000(dh/dt) stays constant.
findings.checked: At h=80 cm and dh/dt=0.1 cm/min, dV/dt=16000 cm³/min=16 L/min and dA/dt=200 cm²/min. These follow from the formulas established in part (a), using methods taught before this question.
findings.assumptions: The trough accommodates the stated depth; the original geometric model continues to apply.

repair.proposal: After p25-q14-c, add (d) “If the depth must increase at 0.1 cm/min, what inflow is required when h=80 cm?” Answer: 16000 cm³/min=16 L/min. (e) “What is the rate of increase of the exposed water surface area at that instant?” Answer: 200 cm²/min. (f) “Explain why doubling the depth from 40 cm to 80 cm doubles the required inflow but leaves the surface-area increase unchanged.” Answer: dV/dt=2000h(dh/dt) depends on h, whereas dA/dt=2000(dh/dt) does not.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects the widening water surface with the inflow needed to maintain a constant depth rate.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening rehearsal of exponential differentiation or solving exponential equations with natural logarithms, although its derivation and worked model use both directly.
findings.breakdown: Following the verification requires the exponential chain factor; fitting the model and finding elapsed time require isolating an exponential and taking logarithms.
findings.checked: The complete earlier teaching concerns polynomial related rates and geometry. Neither prerequisite is rehearsed in the preceding topic. The derivation uses exponential differentiation immediately, and p31-example-demonstration uses logarithms to solve for k and t.
findings.assumptions: These procedures are prior knowledge from the separately listed calculus and exponential/logarithmic courses. A scientific calculator supports numerical evaluation.

repair.proposal: Before p28-introduction, add: (a) Differentiate y=7e^(−3t). Answer: −21e^(−3t). (b) Differentiate y=12−5e^(kt), where k is constant. Answer: −5ke^(kt). (c) Solve 60=20+80e^(5k) for k exactly. Answer: ln(1/2)/5. (d) Solve 25=20+80e^(kt) for t in terms of k, where k<0. Answer: ln(1/16)/k. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Both prerequisite procedures are rehearsed before their use in the modified growth and decay model.

findings.finding: Continue the equal-time predictions to expose the halving of the remaining temperature gap.
findings.breakdown: Equal 45-minute intervals halve the gap to 25°C, so successive temperature increases also halve.
findings.checked: The model is T=25−34e^(−kt), with k=ln(2)/45. Thus T(45)=8, T(90)=16.5 and T(135)=20.75°C. The successive increases are 8.5°C and 4.25°C. Only methods taught by the end of the topic are required.
findings.assumptions: The stated Newton cooling model and constant ambient temperature continue through 135 minutes.

repair.proposal: After p36-q6-c, add (d) “Find the temperature after 135 minutes.” Answer: 20.75°C. (e) “Find the temperature increase from 45 to 90 minutes.” Answer: 8.5°C. (f) “Find the temperature increase from 90 to 135 minutes.” Answer: 4.25°C. (g) “Explain why the second increase is half the first.” Answer: the remaining gap to 25°C halves every 45 minutes.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up distinguishes halving the remaining temperature gap from adding a constant temperature increase.

protectedGroups.observation: The same geometric rate identity can be used in either direction.
protectedGroups.varies: Which rate is supplied and which is required.
protectedGroups.invariant: Circle area and its radius-rate identity.

protectedGroups.observation: A constant radius rate gives the same circumference rate at different radii.
protectedGroups.invariant: Cylinder context, radius rate and requested circumference rate.

protectedGroups.observation: Volume and surface-area rates depend on cube size, while total edge-length rate remains constant.
protectedGroups.varies: Cube size and whether size is supplied as an edge length or volume.
protectedGroups.invariant: The shrinking edge rate and the three requested quantities.

protectedGroups.observation: At the same depth and inflow, changing cone angle changes the rate of rise.
protectedGroups.invariant: Cone context, inflow of 8 cubic centimetres per second and evaluation depth of 4 cm.

protectedGroups.observation: A height of 4 m and a radius of 4 m identify different instants and therefore different rates.
The same geometric derivative relates either choice of known and required ladder rate.
protectedGroups.varies: Known motion, required motion and rate units.

protectedGroups.observation: The volume-depth relationship can determine depth change from inflow or required inflow from depth change.
protectedGroups.varies: The prescribed rate and evaluation depth.

protectedGroups.observation: The signs of both k and A determine direction and limiting behaviour; the sign of k alone does not determine whether Q increases.
protectedGroups.varies: The signs of k and A.
protectedGroups.invariant: The model Q=P+Ae^{kt} and initial-value relationship Q(0)=P+A.

protectedGroups.observation: Exchanging initial and ambient temperatures reverses the sign of A and the direction of change while retaining convergence.
protectedGroups.varies: Which of 25°C and 200°C is the initial value and which is the limiting value.
protectedGroups.invariant: The brownie context, temperature gap of 175°C and convention k<0.

checks.notes: Source and current diagrams visibly supply 120° isosceles cross-section, horizontal water surface, depth h, full depth 3 m and tank length 10 m. Bisecting gives tan30°=h/x, V=10√3h² and A=20√3h. Part (a) constructs volume, (b) supplies area target, (c) provides evaporation law and (d) follows constant dh/dt. Similar-triangle/trigonometric geometry and chain-rule practice precede this closing challenge.

Right triangles and cosine rule yield BG=u cosα, PG=u sinα, AG²=1+u²cos²α-u cosα, then r²=1+u²-u cosα. Part (a) supplies target relation before rate part (b); constant α is stated. This final combined geometry challenge is supported by prior related-rates practice and the opening geometry review.
